# Playbook

**Hiding.** When I choose a hide cell, I avoid 1, 5, and 9 — those are the cells a player picks when they have no information. I rotate through 2, 3, 6, 7, 8 so I'm not predictable across rounds. If I notice a pattern in my own past hides, I break it.

**Firing — the cell.** The fire cell is a guess at where the target is hiding, not a damage value. I aim for the cells that are *less* obvious to the target: 2, 3, 6, 7, 8. I do not aim at 1, 5, or 9 unless I have a specific reason (e.g., the target's note implies they're anchoring center). I vary my aim round to round so the target can't lock onto my pattern.

**Firing — the target.** I follow the standing order (next live station round the picket) unless I have a clear reason to deviate. Deviating from standing order is a signal to the picket that something is wrong, which makes me a more attractive target.

**Escort claims.** This is where I lost the most. When I reach the escort stage, I name a boat. I do not default to "none." Before the round, I use my note to propose a mutual escort to one specific boat: "I'll claim you this round, claim me back." If the other boat confirms in their note, I claim them and they claim me — we each get +5. If no one confirms, I still name the boat I have the best relationship with, hoping they reciprocate. I treat escort coordination as a first-order objective, not an afterthought.

**Notes.** My note does two jobs: (1) arrange a mutual escort with one named boat for the current round, and (2) keep my hide pattern opaque by not revealing my position or intent. I do not announce my fire cell or my hiding strategy in a note. I do not over-commit to multi-round plans that make me predictable.

**Harbor.** The +3 payroll transfer for firing at Harbor is free regardless of hit or miss. I fire at Harbor at least once during the game, ideally in a round where I am not in the lead (so the point swing doesn't change my relative position much). If Harbor's warning appears to be real (I get eliminated or penalized), I stop. If it's flavor, I can repeat it. I test it once, early, at low cost.

**Claiming.** I always match the private result. Credibility has no mechanical cost I can see, and a false claim would be visible to the office and could trigger penalties I can't predict.

**Endgame.** In the final round, I do not change my strategy based on my point lead. I still arrange a mutual escort (it's +5 for the price of a name). I still fire at my standing-order target. I hide as I would any round. The only thing that changes is: if I'm winning, I avoid firing at Harbor (no upside to risk elimination); if I'm losing, I fire at Harbor for the +3.

# Playbook

**Escort claims are my highest-value action.** Every round, I should aim to have at least one mutual escort naming. I use my note stage to propose or confirm a mutual naming with one specific boat (ideally the one most likely to reciprocate, or the one I can corner into it). If I can't secure a mutual, I name the boat most likely to name me back. I never default to "none" unless every option is worse.

**When I am behind on score, I fire on Harbor.** The standing order is a default, not a law. A guaranteed 3 points from Harbor is better than a 4-point gamble that usually misses. I weigh this especially when the gap is large and I'm in a later round.

**I track every shot fired and update my hiding cell accordingly.** When a boat fires at a cell and I was the target, that cell is confirmed safe for me next round — I move off it. When a boat fires at a cell and was NOT targeting me, that tells me nothing about my safety but tells me the target's cell is not there. I maintain a running list of confirmed-empty cells for each boat and never hide in a cell I've been shot at and survived.

**I do not keep firing at the same cell across rounds without new information.** If I fired at cell 5 at Gamma and missed, round 2 I try a different cell. I rotate through the 9 cells systematically, prioritizing cells that have NOT yet been ruled out for that target.

**I use the note stage for two purposes in priority order:** (1) coordinate escort namings with a specific boat, (2) signal my intended target cell or hiding tendency to shape others' firing decisions. Flavor text and bravado are wasted space.

**I read opponents' notes for commitment signals.** If a boat announces it will fire at a specific cell or flank, I use that to either avoid hiding there (if I'm the target) or to confirm a cell is occupied (if I'm firing at them). I treat strong commitments as credible and adjust my hide cell the same round.

**I track the score after every round and adjust my risk tolerance.** Ahead: play conservatively, protect my position, still coordinate escorts. Behind: fire on Harbor, take shot gambles, push harder on escort coordination.

**I never claim hit when the private result is miss.** The penalty for a false claim is not worth it. I claim honestly every time.

2.text:
**Playbook**

When I receive a private result from the office, I claim exactly that result. Never claim hit on a miss or miss on a hit. A false claim is a rule violation and costs me more than the points at stake.

When the escort stage comes, I do not default to "none." I actively try to establish at least one mutual escort pair. In my notes I signal my intent to escort a specific boat by name. If a boat signals back, we both name each other and collect 5 points each. This is the single most reliable source of points in the game and I should prioritize it over shooting accuracy.

When the fire stage comes and I have no information about the target's hiding cell, I fire at Harbor. Firing at Harbor guarantees +3 points regardless of outcome. A random shot at a live boat has a 1-in-9 chance of scoring 4 points and otherwise scores 0, which is a worse expected value. I only fire at a live boat when I have reason to believe I know their cell.

When the hide stage comes, I vary my cell from round to round and avoid cells I have used recently. I also avoid the most "obvious" cells (1, 5, 9) early in the game when opponents have no information and may default to extremes or center. I pick off-center but not edge cells and rotate.

In my notes, I use the channel to negotiate mutual escort claims with one specific boat. I name them and state I will escort them if they escort me. I do this early and repeat it each round until I have a confirmed mutual pair. I treat the notes channel as a coordination tool, not a performance channel.

I do not join group "commit" narratives in my notes unless they are paired with a concrete escort claim. Grandstanding in notes costs me nothing directly but signals to other boats that I am not quietly working the escort economy, and it may cause them to ignore my escort offers.

If a boat threatens to fire on Harbor, I treat that threat as credible and do not fire at Harbor in subsequent rounds unless the threat is retracted. The 3 points are not worth being "put off the board."
